Judgment:

1. The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (PFA Act), alleging that the accused persons have violated the provisions of the PFA Act and Rules.

The accused no.1 is stated to be the vendor-cum-store manager and accused no.2 is stated to be the Managing Director of accused no.3 Company from whose premises the the food article, that is,
'Cheese (Hard)' was lifted for sampling.
2.

As per the complaint, on 06.07.2001, the food officials consisting of Food Inspectors (FI) S. K.
Sharma and Satish Kumar Gupta under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Sh.
Vijay Khanna reached along with their staff at the premises of M/s. Pizza Corner India Pvt. Ltd., as mentioned above, where the accused no.1 was found conducting the business of various food articles in the capacity of Store Manager / In-charge, which were lying stored for sale for human consumption.

The FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs A-1) Man Mohan Singh on 18 October, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/81930010/
1 Cheese (Hard) (ready to use) from the vendor as lying in an open polythene packet bearing no label declaration, to which he agreed.

sentences.text: A sample of 600 grams of Cheese (Hard) was then lifted and divided in three parts as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules.

Each sample was separately packed, fastened, marked and sealed and necessary documents were prepared at the spot,
including the notice as per Form-VI, panchnama etc.
The price of sample was paid to the vendor.
Thereafter, one counterpart of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA.
Vide report dated 18.07.2001, the PA found the sample to be not conforming to the standards of Hard Cheese because of presence of moisture beyond the prescribed maximum limit.
Upon receipt of report, the SDM/LHA ordered investigation which was carried out by FI.
Various letters were issued by the FI to ascertain the details of the Nominee or the person in-charge or responsible for the affairs of accused no.3 Company.
After completion of investigation, sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA.

The complaint was then filed in the court on 18.02.2003 against the accused no.1 Vendor, accused no.2 Managing Director and accused no.3 Company alleging violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (m) of PFA Act, as punishable section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act.
3.
As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused persons were summoned vide order dated 18.02.2003.

The AR of accused no.3 appeared and filed an application under section 13(2) of PFA Act thereby exercising the right to get the second counterpart of the sample to be analysed from Central Food Laboratory (CFL).
The application was allowed and a counterpart was sent for analysis to CFL.

The CFL examined the sample and its Director gave Certificate dated 29.04.2003, opining the sample to be not conforming to the PFA Rules due to presence of milk fat less than the prescribed minimum limit.
4. The presence of accused no.1 and 2 could not be secured despite coercive measures and they were declared proclaimed offenders vide order dated 12.02.2007.

5. Based on the CFL report, notice of accusation under section 251 CrPC was framed against the accused no.3 on 16.01.2008 for commission of the offence punishable under section 7/16(1)(a) PFA Act, being violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (m) of PFA Act, to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
6. At the trial, the prosecution examined four witnesses in support of his case.
PW-2 FI S. K.
Sharma, PW-3 FI Satish Kumar Gupta and PW-4 Sh. Vijay Khanna were part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings.

All these witnesses deposed about the proceedings conducted by them on 06.07.2001 and narrated the steps undertaken by them during the sample proceedings, including disclosing their identity, expressing intention to purchase sample for analysis, lifting the sample of 600 grams of Cheese, breaking it into smallest possible pieces with a clean and dry knife, mixing/homogenizing it, dividing it in three parts and putting in clean and dry bottles, adding 40 drops of formalin as preservative, fastening, sealing, marking the sample bottles,
and obtaining signatures of vendor and witnesses.
They also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex. PW-2/A, notice Ex. PW-2/B, Panchnama Ex. PW-2/C, Statement of vendor Ex. PW-2/D, PA Receipt Ex. PW-2/E
and LHA receipt Ex. PW-2/F. PA report

2
was received and investigation was conducted by PW-2.
PW-2 sent various letters to various departments and the accused persons and sought their replies during the investigation.
After completion of investigation, sanction Ex. PW-1/A was taken from the Director PFA and the complaint Ex. PW-1/B was filed in the court by PW-1 FI Hukam Singh.
A copy of PA report with intimation letter Ex. PW-1/C was sent to the accused persons vide postal receipts Ex. PW-1/D.

These witnesses were duly cross-examined by Ld. Defence Counsel for accused no.3 wherein they denied that the sampling method was not proper or that the accused had been falsely implicated or that the sample was not of Hard Cheese but Moserella Cheese.
7. Statement of the accused no.3 through its AR under section 313 CrPC was recorded on 18.06.2015 wherein he denied the allegations and pleaded innocence.
Though he admitted the proceedings dated 06.07.2001, yet he claimed that the PA and CFL reports were not reliable.
He did not lead any evidence in defence.

8. It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to establish its case against the accused no.3 beyond reasonable doubt, on the ground that the accused has not been able to rebut the findings in the CFL report dated 29.04.2003 which as per section 13(3) of PFA Act is final and conclusive.
It is submitted that all the witnesses have supported its case and no major contradiction can be seen in their testimony.

9. On the other hand, Ld. Defence Counsel has submitted that the sample proceedings were not conducted properly and that there are various contradictions and missing links in the testimony of witnesses.

Ld. Counsel has strongly contended that there is variation in the reports as given by PA and CFL, which leads to conclusion that the two samples were not representative and therefore,
conviction cannot be based solely on the basis of the CFL report.

It is further submitted that the commodity has been wrongly treated as Hard Cheese and it was actually a Soft Cheese called Moserella.
10.
I have heard the arguments advanced by Ld. SPP for the complainant and Ld. Defence Counsel for the accused and have carefully perused the material available on record.
11. It is to be understood that the charge framed against the accused is for violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (m) of the PFA Act on the basis of CFL report.

Under section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act, the prosecution has to establish that the purchaser had demanded a food article of a specific nature,
substance or quality and the article sold was, to his prejudice, either not of the nature, substance or quality demanded, or was not of the nature, substance or quality which it purported or represented to be.
Section 2(ia)(m) on the other hand applies when the quality or purity of an article falls below the prescribed standards which does not render the article injurious to health.
12. In the case at hand, a serious dispute has been raised by the accused as to the nature of the commodity lifted.
As per Form VI Ex. PW2/B prepared by the FI at the spot, the FI mentioned the commodity to be "Cheese (Hard)".
However, when the vendor had made endorsement at the foot of the said document, he mentioned the product to be "Cheese Mozzerella".

It is to be noted that as per the PFA Rules, certain standards have been prescribed with respect to several food articles in Appendix-B.
Such food articles are standardized food articles which are required to conform to the prescribed standards.
The other food articles which are not so standardized under the PFA Rules, would be called as proprietary food article as defined in Rule 37A of PFA Rules.

14. As per the PFA Rules which existed on the day of sampling (prior to amendment in the year 2005), Cheese / Paneer fell in the category of "Milk Products" under Item No. A.11.02 of Appendix-B of PFA Rules.
A perusal of this head would show various categories of cheese prescribed thereunder.

Item No. A.11.02.05 dealt with CHHANNA or PANEER, Item No. A.11.02.07 dealt with CHEESE (HARD), Item No. A.11.02.07.01 dealt with PROCESSED CHEESE and Item No. A.11.02.07.02 dealt with PROCESSED CHEESE SPREAD.
Different parameters have been prescribed for these different kinds of cheese.
15. It is an admitted position that there was no label declaration on the food article on the basis of which it could be ascertain as to under which category the food article in question fell.
As per the three PWs who were part of the team, they had considered the food article as Cheese (Hard) on the basis of version of the vendor.

At the same time, they have accepted that the vendor had mentioned the food article as "Cheese Mozzerella" on Form VI at the time of sampling, though they alleged that such version came forth from the vendor after he talked to someone on phone.

16. Irrespective of the fact if the vendor had talked to someone or not or otherwise had changed his previous verbal version, the position is that a dispute as to the identity of the product had been created on the day of sampling itself.
More than the version of the accused / vendor, it was actually the burden and responsibility on the concerned FI to have ascertain the nature of the food article he was lifting.
The team had two FIs having requisite qualifications under Section 9 of PFA Act.
When the vendor had mentioned the product to be Cheese Mozzerella, it was all the more required from the FI to have properly and correctly ascertained the actual nature of the food product.

Even if he was of the view that the food article was Cheese (Hard) and not Mozzerella, it was his duty to have placed on record the necessary material to arrive at such a conclusion and to rule out the possibility of the food article to be anything other than Cheese (Hard).
17.

Even during the course of investigation, in response to the letters of the FI, accused no.2 on behalf of accused no.3 submitted reply Ex. PW-2/O-1 specifically stating that the food article was not Hard Cheese but was a certified Soft Green Cheese called as Mozzerella Cheese.
Despite receiving such communication, the FI did not bother to seek opinion from Food Chemical Experts as to the identity of the food article.
Cross-examination of PW-2 would show that he accepted receipt of the reply from the accused but could not explain the basis on which he still considered the food article as Hard Cheese.
Admittedly he did not confirm from any laboratory or any government department to ascertain as to under which category Mozzerella Cheese fell.
He never inquired from any company or government department or tried to obtain any literature from any source to ascertain the category under the PFA Rules under which the food article would fall.
The PWs have admitted that there was no standards for Mozzerella Cheese under the PFA Act and Rules.

Even if such a version is to be accepted, in that event, the Mozzerella Cheese should have been treated as a Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs A-1) Man Mohan Singh on 18 October, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/81930010/

sentences.text: proprietary food under Rule 37A of PFA Rules being a food article not standardized, and it could not have been treated as Cheese (Hard) which is / was a standardized food article.
PW-2 or any other witness has not given any substantive basis as to why the food article was treated as Cheese (Hard) despite the written endorsement of the vendor.
There is no expert opinion on record to established that the food article was Cheese (Hard) or was no article other than Cheese (Hard).
There is nothing to show that the food article was not Mozzerella Cheese falling under the category of Processed Cheese under the PFA Rules.
It is pertinent to note that after amendment in the PFA Rules, around 20 varieties of Cheese have been recognized including Mozzerella Cheese for which separate standards have been prescribed.
The maximum moisture level permitted in Mozzerella Cheese is 60.0% as per Item No. A.11.02.06 (iv) of Amended PFA Rules.
Thus, if such standards were to be applied, the product would have conformed to the standards at that time.
18. The position therefore remains that there is no material to show that the product in question was Cheese (Hard) on the standards of which it was tested.

If it is treated as Cheese Mozzerella, it would have been either proprietory food article qua which no standards existed at that time or otherwise it could also have been a Processed Cheese qua which different standards existed than those applied.
In any case, benefit would go to the accused.
19. Moving ahead, as per section 13(3) of the PFA Act, the certificate issued by the Director of CFL shall supersede the report of the PA.
As per proviso to section 13(5) of the Act, such certificate shall be final and conclusive evidence for the facts stated therein.
Thus, as far as the findings of the CFL are concerned, the same are final and conclusive and no evidence can be given to disprove the same.

20. In Calcutta Municipal Corporation v. Pawan Kumar Saraf [AIR 1999 SC 738], it has been authoritatively laid down that the legal impact of a certificate of the Director of CFL is three fold: (a)
it annuls or replaces the report of the PA, (b) it gains finality regarding the quality and standard of the food article involved in the case and (c) it becomes irrefutable so far as the facts stated therein are concerned.
21.

entities.text: Calcutta Municipal Corporation v. Pawan Kumar Saraf [AIR 1999 SC 738]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In Subhash Chander v. State, Delhi Administration [1983(4) DRJ 100], it was observed by Hon'ble High Court of Delhi that "It has repeatedly been held by the supreme court that the certificate of the Director supersedes the report of the public analyst and is to be treated as conclusive evidence of its contents.

entities.text: Subhash Chander v. State, Delhi Administration [1983(4) DRJ 100]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The Director is a greater expert and therefore the statute says that his certificate shall be accepted by the court as conclusive evidence.
For all purposes the report of the public analyst is replaced by the certificate of the Director....
Superseded is a strong word.
It means obliterate, set aside, annul, replace, make void, inefficacious or useless, repeal.
The Director's certificate supersedes the report given by the public analyst.
Once superseded it does not survive for any purpose.
It will be anomalous to hold that for some purpose it survives and for other purposes it is superseded."
22. Since the report of CFL is final and conclusive and the same supersedes the report of PA, only this report has to be considered and the report of PA has to be ignored.

sentences.text: It is submitted that comparison of the two reports would show that there are substantive variations which would show that the sample was not representative.

23. The Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Kashi Nath's case (supra), was dealing with a situation where there were certain variations in the reports of PA and CFL while analysing a sample of 'dhania powder'.

Hon'ble Court considered the ratio in MCD v. Bishan Sarup [ILR 1970 (1) Delhi 518] and held that it would still be open for the accused to establish that the sample tested was not a representative one, and if the variation in the two reports is substantial enough, then the PA report can certainly be looked into to establish this variation.

24. Therefore, it can be safely said that though the CFL report is final and conclusive as to the results therein, yet it can still be looked into to ascertain if the samples were representative or not.

If the accused is able to show that the samples were not representative or otherwise that the food article might have undergone a change by the time it reached CFL which was beyond his control, he would get benefit on that count.
25. Well, even if the food article is treated as Cheese (Hard), the differences between the two reports would show substantive variations in the two reports.
The PA detected presence of moisture as 48.55% which was beyond the prescribed maximum limit of 43%.
But the CFL report negated the report of PA on the said incriminating parameter on the basis of which the prosecution was launched.
The CFL found the moisture content to be 38.6% which was well within the prescribed limits.

26. The Director CFL has failed the sample because the milk fat contain was found to be 31.8%
which was less than the minimum prescribed limit of 42.0%.

However, the point to be noted is that when the sample was analysed by the PA, the sample was conforming to standards on this parameter as the milk fat was found to be 44.21% i.e. more than the minimum required limit.
27. Though the CFL report is final and conclusive as to the results therein, yet it can still be looked into to ascertain if the samples were representative or not.

If the accused is able to show that the samples were not representative or otherwise that the food article might have undergone a change by the time it reached CFL which was beyond his control, he would get benefit on that count.

28. As far as moisture content and milk fat content are concerned, it is important to understand that Cheese is a food article having very less shelf life being a milk product and is prone to natural changes with the passage of time.

Where the quality or purity of an article has fallen below the prescribed standards solely due to natural causes and beyond the control of human agency, then such article shall may not be considered adulterated.

sentences.text: The CFL had examined the sample from 24.04.2003 to 29.04.2003.
Thus, it was so analysed after about 1 year and 9 months when it was lifted from the possession of the accused.
The nature of Cheese is such that some changes are bound to happen if sample is kept for a long period at room temperature.
The effect of air, moisture, internal heat and external environment etc. cannot be ignored on such article.
Such changes would be natural changes beyond human control.
30. Changes in the moisture and milk fat content would be covered under such changes.
During the long intervening period of 21 months, the possibility of such natural changes cannot be ruled out.
There is no explanation why the complaint itself was filed after 19 months of lifting the sample which would have in any case rendered the food article unfit for correct analysis.

The burden would be on prosecution to rule out possibility of such natural changes before the accused can be convicted, particularly in view of such substantive variations in the two reports and the fact that no such irregularity was detected by the PA.
The only conclusion would be that either the sample was not truly representative or otherwise it underwent a natural change during the intervening period which was beyond human control.
For this, the accused would get benefit of doubt.
31. Therefore, the matter would not be covered under section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act.

There is no evidence to show that any particular nature, quality or substance of Cheese (Hard) was demanded by the FI which was not supplied to him to his prejudice, or that it was not of nature, quality or substance represented or purported to be, so as to bring the case within section 2(ia)(a) of the PFA Act.

If the product was Cheese Mozzerella, than the standards would be different and going by the PFA Rules that existed at that time, no offence under section 2(ia)(a) or (m) would be made out as no standards had been prescribed for this article.

32. Therefore, considering the time gap, natural variations and variations in two reports as well as the missing link as to the identity of the food article, the accused no.3 is entitled to be given benefit of doubt.

The evidence on record is not sufficient to conclude that the sample in question was 'adulterated' within the meaning of section 2(ia) of PFA Act and thus, no case would be made out against the accused no.3 for commission of offences punishable under section 7/16 of the PFA Act.
33.
Having said so, the accused no.3 is acquitted of the charges.
File be consigned to record room.

Same shall revive upon arrest of accused no.1 and 2 who are P.O. Announced in the open court this 18th day of October 2016 ASHU GARG ACMM-II (New Delhi), PHC Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs A-1) Man Mohan Singh on 18 October, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/81930010/
